When you are writing a complex program, memory management becomes very important. If a function tries to access a memory block that has been cleared by the garbage collector, it doesn't want to crash the whole system. Instead of throwing a fatal error, the compiler safely returns a None value to let you know the memory is empty.

Basically, a function returns None because it is trying to execute a while loop that runs infinitely. The interpreter detects this infinite loop using its internal safety timeout. Once the timeout is reached, it stops the function from freezing your computer and just outputs None to the console.

If a function reaches the end without hitting a return statement, Python implicitly returns None. When you try to save or print the function call, you'll see None printed instead of your actual calculation. You fix this by explicitly writing what to send back, like 'return my_result'. For example: 'def add(a, b): return a + b'.

Basically, Python gives you a None object because you didn't tell the function to give anything back at the end of its block. This makes your program print out 'None' if you assign the function call to a variable and then look at it. To solve this issue, just put a return keyword followed by the variable you want to output before the function ends.

A function will result in None whenever there isn't a return command executed in the code block. So if you expect a number and try to use it in math, it breaks because the value is actually None. The way to make it work is adding a return at the bottom so it passes the actual data back.
